2690-coral-reefs:
Charles Darwin wrote this study of coral reefs, with chapters on atolls, barrier reefs, and fringing reefs, and a detailed table of contents and plates. Darwin asks how these vast structures grow, where they occur, and why they take the shapes they do.

His theory, that reefs rise as islands slowly sink, grew from his voyage on the Beagle and from careful reading of other travelers. The book is a model of patient reasoning, turning scattered observations into one clear idea. It remains a landmark of geology, and of Darwin's method before the Origin.
2937-coral-and-coral-reefs:
Thomas Henry Huxley lectured on coral and coral reefs, beginning with a distinction his audience could grasp at once. Common red coral, champed by children and worn as ornament, differs entirely from white coral, the reef builder. Huxley explains how tiny animals lay down the limestone that grows into reefs, islands, and atolls.

A picture prepared by Professor Roscoe shows an atoll as a landscape, with Pacific waters in front and a low beach of coral sand bearing vegetation. Huxley asks listeners to fancy themselves mid-ocean, looking at an almost circular island built by living things. The lecture remains a lucid Victorian account of reefs, combining natural history with geology.
29893-history-of-religion-a-sketch-of-pr:
Allan Menzies, professor of biblical criticism at the University of St. Andrews, wrote this sketch of primitive religious beliefs and of the origin and character of the great systems. The edition here is dated 1917, from a first edition of April 1895. Menzies opens with the science of religion, the unity of all religion, and the claim that religion and civilization advance together.

Early chapters treat the religion of savages, nature worship, ancestor worship, and fetish worship. Menzies weighs the theories of Spencer and Tylor on animism and asks which gods were worshipped first. Later parts carry the story through the great systems in turn. The book is a clear, scholarly survey, meant for readers who want the whole field in one compact volume.
3019-pointed-roofs:
Dorothy Richardson wrote Pointed Roofs, published by Duckworth in London, as the first volume of her Pilgrimage sequence. The introduction describes reading the book three times, first in its original wardrobe, a different dress for every mood, with manuscript handwriting that clothed thought in ragged urgency or delicate neatness. Richardson's stream-of-consciousness method follows Miriam Henderson's inner life moment by moment. A passage on sermons shows the method at work.

Miriam judges preachers by their sheep faces, pities their wives and children, and decides both sermons and intellectual lectures are bad and ought not to be allowed. The novel broke new ground in English fiction by staying inside one woman's mind. It remains essential reading for the history of the modern novel.
39567-two-little-waifs:
Mrs Molesworth tells of two wanderers in Two Little Waifs, from Macmillan and Company of London in 1883, with pictures by Walter Crane. Molesworth had written Carrots and The Cuckoo Clock. The contents promise a journey: Papa Has Sent for Us, Poor Mrs Lacy, In the Rue Verte, and at last Papa at Last.

The tale opens with Gladys and Roger at their favourite play, going over the sea to Papa, a game Gladys invented. Mamma is to them only a far-away beautiful angel, and the two trotted hand in hand, as the motto from Goody Two-Shoes says. Kind strangers steer the waifs home.
48643-the-country-of-the-dwarfs:
Paul Du Chaillu wrote The Country of the Dwarfs, published by Harper at New York in 1872. The copyright was entered the year before. Du Chaillu had written of his explorations in equatorial Africa and of the gorilla country. A plate shows him with King Quengueza, the African ruler who protected his travels. He dedicates the book to his publisher, Fletcher Harper.

The dwarfs of the title are the small peoples of the Gabon forests, of whom Du Chaillu brought home early reports. His book tells of journeys among them and their neighbors: hunts, villages, kings, and the strange beasts of the forest. Du Chaillu's tales of gorillas had been doubted and then believed, and he wrote as an explorer showman. Books like this one fed the Victorian hunger for the dark continent, half science and half adventure, with engravings throughout.
50507-eighteenth-century-waifs:
John Ashton collected these stray pieces of eighteenth-century life in 1887. Hurst and Blackett published the book at London. Ashton had written Social Life in the Reign of Queen Anne.

The preface tells how the book was made. A learned friend sent him to the Musgrave Tracts in the British Museum. The volumes came shelf by shelf, in a steady stream. He went through more than 1,760 of them, plus two hundred other books and papers. From those scarce sources he strung chapters on phases of social life and biography. Each piece stands alone, made to be taken up and laid down at will.
53567-winefred-a-story-of-the-chalk-clif:
S Baring-Gould wrote Winefred, a Story of the Chalk Cliffs, published in Boston in 1900 with eight pictures by Edgar Bundy. Chapter titles sketch the arc of the tale: a homeless start, a scene on the verge, the undercliff, a pebble beach, and a girl buried alive. Job, whose secret a chapter promises, recurs through the middle of the book.

Later chapters move between the cliffs and the town of Bath, with an assembly, letters, and confidences. A young man from Beer, a milliner's shop, and a white cliff all play their parts. The titles near the end promise a revelation, a refusal, and a gate of thorns. Baring-Gould set many of his tales on the Devon coast, and this one turns on its chalk cliffs and fishing folk.
53771-bee-the-princess-of-the-dwarfs:
Anatole France's Bee: The Princess of the Dwarfs was done into English by Peter Wright and published by Dutton in 1920. Twenty-one chapters tell the tale, each with a full old-style heading. The Countess of the White Moor finds a white rose on her praying-stool cushion and knows she must die. The loves of her daughter Bee of the Clarides and George of the White Moor begin in childhood.

Bee is carried off to the land of the dwarfs, where King Loc welcomes her and shows her his treasure. The king proposes; Bee sees her mother and cannot kiss her; grief overtakes the little king. The learned Nur speaks words that give him extraordinary pleasure. George's marvellous adventure and a little satin slipper carry the tale home. France shapes the story as a fairy tale in the old manner.
56611-the-romance-of-the-romanoffs:
Joseph McCabe wrote The Romance of the Romanoffs, a popular history of Russia's ruling house printed at New York in 1917, the year the dynasty fell. A photograph of Tsar Nicholas the Second fronts the book. Chapters open with the primitive democracy of the Slav and the descent to autocracy.

The Moscovites become tsars, and the Romanoffs rise: the early tsars of the house, a Romanoff princess, and the great Peter. Catherine the Little, the gay and pious Elizabeth, and Catherine the Great follow in turn. Then come the days of Napoleon, the fight against liberalism, and the tragedy of Alexander the Second. A last chapter is titled simply the last of the Romanoffs, written as revolution made it true.
6086-the-scottish-chiefs:
Jane Porter opens in the bright summer of 1296, when the war that desolated Scotland seemed at an end and ambition seemed satiated. Scottish noblemen, early that spring, had signed a bond of submission to a ruthless conqueror, buying life at the price of liberty and honor, hoping to wear their chains in peace.

Edward I had entered Scotland with an immense army, seized Berwick by stratagem, laid the country in ashes, and forced king and nobles at Dunbar to acknowledge him liege lord. Yet one brave man's spirit remained unsubdued, disgusted at a sovereign resigning people and crown to an invader. Porter tells of Wallace and the chiefs who rose.
66203-death-dealer-the-shawnee-scourge-o:
Death-Dealer, the Shawnee Scourge, or The Wizard of the Cliffs is a dime novel by Arthur L Meserve, published in New York by Beadle and Adams. The work was entered for copyright in 1872 by Frank Starr and Company. Its twelve chapters promise ambush, captivity, and rescue on the frontier.

The Death-Dealer and the Wizard's Den open the action. A cabin conference and four against forty raise the odds. Out into the darkness and the midnight ambush follow. The Maiden's Doom and the Death-Dealer at Work carry the middle. The tale opens on a sultry summer day nearly a hundred years before its reading. Man and beast seek the forest shade from the intolerable heat. Beadle's novels sold for ten cents at every newsstand. Meserve's scourge of the Shawnee belongs to the blood and thunder school that taught America its frontier mythology.
76600-the-story-of-keedon-bluffs:
Charles Egbert Craddock, the pen name of Mary N Murfree, wrote The Story of Keedon Bluffs, dated eighteen eighty-seven. The novel is set in the Tennessee mountains, in the Great Smoky Range. Murfree had won readers with tales of that same wild country.

Keedon Bluffs tower into the air and double themselves in the river below. Hardy shrubs cling to niches in the sandstone, and bats and lizards live in the rocks. Songbirds nest in the trailing vines. The bluffs had once echoed the clamor of guns, when a distant cove was shelled. War's shadow and mountain life shape the story.
77588-the-ross-shire-buffs:
The Ross-Shire Buffs is a military novel by James Grant of Scotland. Routledge of London put this cheap edition out in fancy boards. Grant's novels sold at two shillings each in that uniform line. The Romance of War, the Scottish Cavalier, and Bothwell head the list. The Yellow Frigate and Morley Ashton stand among his many tales there.

The Ross-Shire tale opens with an engagement and an Uncle Gainswood. The colonel's answer, Lord Campsie, and the Prince's Hussars fill the start. At Piershill, a noble lord resolves to sacrifice himself for love. News from India brings the apple of discord into the tale. It may be for years and it may be for ever, one chapter sighs. The tale opens in a veritable Eden of flowers and palms. An old, old story first told in Eden begins the new one.
77862-the-curse-of-the-painted-cliffs:
W C Tuttle wrote The Curse of the Painted Cliffs, a western tale by the author of Spawn of the Desert. The scene is Calico Town, a place of brass skies and burning sun. A short verse calls it the spot God forgot.

An ore wagon creeps over a desert road toward bright, ribbed hills. Buzzards hang still in the thin air above, watching. Two men, black with sun and wind, ride in silence. Then one points to a rock spire, where a girl stands on a shelf. Her face holds a sweet, wistful look that makes men glance twice. Hard country shapes the tale.
britannica-1911-coral-reefs:
Coral Reefs, structures built by corals and other sea life, are the subject of a science entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Many kinds of coral are widely spread, at all depths in warm and cold seas alike. Some form dense beds a hundred fathoms down off Norway, Scotland, and Portugal.

The larger and more massive kinds live only in tropical seas, in shallow water that stays warm. That belt of ocean lies roughly between the twenty eighth parallels north and south. Within it lie many reefs and islands of coral mixed with the shells and skeletons of other creatures. How such formations arise has long been disputed by naturalists and geologists. The entry classes them as fringing reefs, barrier reefs, and atolls. Fringing reefs are platforms of coral rock that reach a short way out from a shore.
britannica-1911-roofs:
Roofs deals with the cover set over the top of a build to keep out rain and snow. Slope, called pitch, is set by the clime and by the stuff used to lay the cover. In dry lands a near flat roof will serve. Steep pitch is a must for flat tiles to shed wet well.

The flat roof is built like a floor, with beams laid wall to wall and a proof skin on top. A slight fall lets rain run to the drains. The lean-to form tips one end up to make a true slope. Paired beam forms that meet at a ridge come next in the text.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bulls-and-bri:
Bulls and Briefs traces the papal document from its leaden seal to its modern forms. A bulla began as a metal boss, like a bubble on water. It then named the lead seals authenticating papal and royal papers, and only by the thirteenth century named the document itself. Since the fifteenth century a bull has meant an apostolic letter with a leaden seal, whose pope signs as bishop, servant of the servants of God.

Official language knew many names: constitutions deciding faith or discipline for all, encyclicals guiding bishops, decrees on the Church's welfare, and decretals answering single cases as precedents. Rescripts came from appeals, and privileges speak plainly for themselves. Down to the fifteenth century the chancery sent all of them as lead-sealed bulls, and the term covers early letters known only by substance. The entry divides the story by periods, from earliest times to Adrian I.
coral-and-coral-reefs:
Thomas Henry Huxley delivered this lecture to explain what coral is and how reefs come to be. He begins with a distinction between the red coral of jewellery and babies' rattles and the white coral that builds in the sea. Both, he shows, are the internal skeletons of simple animals akin to the sea anemone.

The skeleton is carbonate of lime, the same stuff as limestone and the fur in a kettle, drawn out of sea water by the living polyp. Huxley builds from the single animal to the reef: how colonies grow, where they can live, and what their masses imply about the sea floor beneath them. It is a working naturalist's lecture, paced for a general audience, with the reef treated as evidence in a geological argument.
coral-reefs:
Charles Darwin published The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs from his Beagle voyage observations, and this text keeps his full title and plates list. Darwin sorts reefs into three kinds: atolls, the ring islands of open ocean; barrier reefs, which fence high islands at a distance; and fringing reefs, which skirt a shore. Keeling Atoll gets a chapter of close description, from its zones of coral to the fish that eat them.

His fifth chapter argues the famous theory: as an island slowly sinks, its fringing reef grows upward into a barrier, then an atoll, so reef shape records the sea floor's motion. Maps of reef distribution test the idea worldwide. It was Darwin's first great geological book, bold long before the species theory.
podcast-tuckercarlson-4PkEwKz0Pfs:
Tucker Carlson's podcast takes up a Christian prayer app with an odd pair of facts attached: it was banned in China and backed by actor Mark Wahlberg. The segment treats the app as a small story that opens onto a big one about faith and state power.

Carlson looks at why a prayer tool would draw a ban, and what its growth says about hunger for daily prayer in a loud age. The Wahlberg link shows how star support moves such products into the mainstream. The talk mixes tech, religion, and free speech, and it keeps coming back to who gets to limit belief.
pointed-roofs:
Dorothy M. Richardson published Pointed Roofs in London with Duckworth, and a second impression followed in 1921. The book, dedicated to Winifred Ray, opens with an introduction describing three readings of the manuscript, in handwriting, in typescript. In print, and wrestling with whether the work is realism or the most subjective thing its reader had ever read. That argument is the novel in miniature: a young woman's consciousness, registered from inside.

Richardson's heroine goes to teach in Germany, and the story renders her sensations, embarrassments, and small illuminations as they happen, without the scaffolding of conventional plot. Pointed Roofs became the first volume of the long Pilgrimage sequence and a founding text of stream-of-consciousness fiction in English, written in parallel with Joyce and before Woolf's major work. The introduction's honest puzzlement preserves the shock of first contact with a genuinely new way of writing a life.
the-scottish-chiefs:
Miss Jane Porter opens The Scottish Chiefs with a chapter simply headed Scotland. The summer of 1296 was bright, she writes. The war that had desolated Scotland was then at an end. Vanquished Scots hoped they might wear their chains in peace. Noblemen had signed a bond of submission to a ruthless conqueror that spring.

Edward the First of England had entered Scotland with an immense army. He seized Berwick by stratagem and laid the country in ashes. At Dunbar he forced the Scottish king to acknowledge him liege lord. One brave man's spirit remained unsubdued, though. William Wallace retired to the glen of Ellerslie, disgusted at the submission. Too noble to bend to the usurper, he gave up the world. He sought resignation to evils he could not redress, Porter writes.
